Q: Tell LLDB to ignore files A:

There is a setting to avoid stepping into functions whose name match a regular expression,

(lldb) settings list target.process.thread.step-avoid-regexp
step-avoid-regexp -- A regular expression defining functions step-in won't stop in.

e.g. put this in your ~/.lldbinit file

settings set target.process.thread.step-avoid-regexp ^[^ ]+ std::|^std::

but in Xcode 4.5.x that's the best that can be done. I mentioned in #2 of your links that inlined stepping support has been added to the LLDB sources at http://lldb.llvm.org/ but that won't be in Xcode until the next release.

Q: What exactly does AI do beyond ML models and rule-based logic? A:

It is true that Machine Learning is an integral part of AI and the fact that behind most of the AI-based applications on internet there are indeed heavily trained ML models (such as generative AI, image creation, predictions, etc.). However, there do exist some instances of things being AI but not ML. Before I list such examples, one point to note is that AI broadly aims at imitating human behavior/performing tasks that require human intervention.
Example 1: Automated rule-based trading system
There exist rule-based automated stock market trading systems whose task is to place orders based on an already calculated and well-defined trading strategy based on market signals. Although there exist some systems which make use of ML, but rule-based systems have got nothing to do with ML. All they do is to extract market data and place order as per the calculations. Since these tasks do require human intervention and that they have been automated, this is certainly in the AI domain but not ML.
Example 2: Chess Engines
Although this might not be applicable to all of the modem-day chess engines, but a lot of popular chess engines (such as Deep blue) are based on minimax-algorithm which is basically a static code that is able to calculate the best move based on a given position. This has got nothing to do with Machine Learning as here they calculate the best move and not predict it. Since these engines imitate human behavior, by making their moves, they are also in the AI domain but not ML.

Q: Page-break-inside:avoid not working A:

Different browsers have weird limitations for page-break-inside: avoid. Following limitations have been suggested in many different articles. My summary follows:

  • If the document tree has the parent or grandparent with display:flex or display:grid, avoiding page-breaks will not work.
  • If the parent element has display:inline-block, avoid doesn't work.
  • In some cases, parent element needs position:relative for the value avoid to work in children. (Exact rules unknown.)
  • In some cases, both the parent element and the element that needs to avoid breaking needs position:relative for the value avoid to work. (Exact rules unknown.)
  • The parent element MUST NOT have display: inline-block.
  • The element MUST NOT have display:table-cell.

In short, @media print styles should probably avoid using float, flex, grid, position:absolute and position:sticky if you need to use page-break-inside: avoid. For best compatibility with different browsers, try to define whole tree from root to parent with display:block and the element that shouldn't break with display:inline-block in addition to page-break-inside: avoid.

None of the above exceptions are part of any specs so these are just bugs or limitations in browser implementations.

Also note that even though latest specs prefer break-inside: avoid instead of page-break-inside: avoid the real world browser supports is still pretty bad. I would recommend declaring both:

.nobreak
{
  page-break-inside: avoid;
  break-inside: avoid
}
